podcast.title: Intentional Speaker Damage for Distortion (1964)
podcast.body: Dave Davies was an early pioneer in physically modifying amplifiers to achieve distortion. In 1964, while recording a song with The Kinks, he intentionally damaged the speaker cone of his small amplifier, using either a razor blade or a screwdriver, to produce a distorted sound. While effective in creating the desired effect, this method offered little control over the specific type or intensity of the distortion. "When the band was recording this song in 1964, he slashed the speaker cone of his small amp."

podcast.title: Amplifier Modification for Distortion
podcast.body: Frustrated with the sound of his amplifier, Dave Davis took a knife and "slashed the cone." He then fed the sound from this modified, "slashed amp" through his "new larger amp" to achieve a distinctively "distorted, fuzzy sound." This innovative technique was "almost unknown in Britain at the time" and is considered a pivotal moment in standardizing distorted guitar as a rock element. "Dave had been frustrated with the sound he was getting from his amplifier and had slashed the cone with a knife."

podcast.title: Big Bill Broonzy Influence
podcast.body: A 16-minute documentary, "Low Light and Blue Smoke," detailing Big Bill Broonzy's tour of Belgium, was a "defining moment of inspiration" for Dave, as it was for Ray, showcasing an authentic sound that resonated deeply. "a defining moment of inspiration for both brothers, came when a 16 minute documentary about Big Bill Roons' tour of Belgium, Low Light and Blue Smoke, was shown on the TV."

podcast.title: Bisexuality
podcast.body: Dave Davis is explicitly stated to be bisexual. This aspect of his sexuality, combined with Ray's tendency to explore gender and sexuality, influenced manager Larry Page's decision to subtly alter the lyrics of "You Really Got Me" to "girl you really got me going" to potentially reassure the public. "Dave Davis is bisexual, and Ray has always been keen to play around with notions of gender and sexuality."

podcast.title: DIY Amp Modification
podcast.body: Dave Davies, frustrated with not getting the right sound from his Vox Elpico amp during a recording session for The Kinks, intentionally hacked up its speaker cone with a razor blade and poked holes in it with a pin. This extreme modification was a deliberate effort to achieve a specific distorted sound. "But not before Brother Dave Davies hacked up the speaker code of his Vox Elpico amp with a razor blade and poking some holes in it with a pin for good measure."

podcast.title: Developing Guitar Prowess
podcast.body: After Ray's temporary departure to play with jazz musicians, Dave, Pete, and John continued rehearsing, and Dave "would become a far more accomplished guitarist, now outshining his brother." He also began engaging more deeply with the London R&B scene, further honing his skills. "Dave would become a far more accomplished guitarist, now outshining his brother, and was also getting more into the London R&B scene."

podcast.title: Difficult Sibling Relationship
podcast.body: Dave, three years younger than Ray, had a "difficult relationship" with his older brother. While Dave "always looked up to his older brother," he "never really got to know him," reflecting the complex and "diametrically opposed personalities" within the duo. "Dave always looked up to his older brother, but never really got to know him."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Early Collaboration with Ray (Cynical Motivation)
podcast.body: In their youth, Dave looked up to his older brother Ray and valued his opinion. Ray exploited this by telling Dave which new records were good, prompting Dave to buy them so Ray could play them while saving his own pocket money for other things. "Dave would go out and buy them, and then Ray could play them and spend his own money on other things."

podcast.title: Early Vocal Performances
podcast.body: In the Ray Davis Quartet, Dave would sometimes sing lead vocals, specializing in "upbeat rockers" and material from artists like Little Richard and Lightning Hopkins. "Dave would take the lead vocals on most of the upbeat Rutgers, and Ray and Dave would sing Udison Leeds on everything else."

podcast.title: Instant Dislike of Mick Avory
podcast.body: When Mick Avory was chosen as the Kinks' permanent drummer by Ray and the management, Dave Davis took an "instant dislike to him." This aversion was partly because Ray liked Avory, though Dave ultimately "accepted that he was the best drummer available." podcast.title: Lead Guitar on Early Kinks Records
podcast.body: It is "definitely not in doubt" that Dave Davis played "all the lead guitar" on the Kinks' early recordings, even amidst disputes regarding who played Ray Davis's rhythm parts. "What's definitely not in doubt is that Dave Davis played all the lead guitar."

podcast.title: Songwriting for Sean Aile
podcast.body: Dave Davis wrote the song "One Fine Day," which was recorded by Sean Aile, with Shell Tauhmey producing. While the transcript dismisses it as a "throwaway," it is noted as being "actually quite catchy." "With Townley producing, Sean Aile recorded Dave's One Fine Day, a song which it's right to dismisses as a throwaway, but is actually quite catchy."

podcast.title: The Ventures Influence
podcast.body: In the early days of the Ray Davis Quartet, Dave particularly enjoyed performing "No Trespassing" by The Ventures, indicating an early influence of instrumental guitar bands on his musical preferences. "The group mostly performed in Strentleles, with Dave particularly enjoying playing no trespassing by the ventures."

podcast.title: Trauma of Separation from Daughter
podcast.body: At age 15, Dave impregnated his 16-year-old girlfriend, Susan Fregnant. Despite their love and desire to marry, both sets of parents, "horrified," intervened by falsely telling each child that the other had dumped them. Both believed the lie, resulting in Dave not seeing his daughter for 30 years. This separation "permanently changed him," and its "echoes" can be found throughout his songwriting in the 1960s. "Dave didn't see his daughter for 30 years. The trauma of this separation permanently changed him, and you can find echoes of it throughout Dave's songwriting in the 60s."

xref.title: Previous Reigning Champions of Sibling Rivalry
xref.body: Before Liam and Noel Gallagher, Ray and Dave Davies of The Kinks were considered the benchmark for intense and long-standing sibling rivalries in music. Their continuous feuding was widely known and documented. "Even crazier than what we've seen with Ray and Dave Davies of the Kinks, the previous reigning champions."
